situation:
You are the financial analyst at NORTHRIDGE COLD CHAIN, a cold storage logistics provider that freezes and holds goods for regional food producers. The chief executive officer (judge) took over fourteen months ago after two straight years of losses, and has asked you to recommend how the company should free the cash its own operations have locked up.

The company's cash sits in two places. Customers owe close to eighty days of invoices, well past the thirty days the contracts allow, even though new tracking software now sends every invoice the hour a load leaves the dock. The rest is tied up in a warehouse of spare compressors, coils and pallet racking that earlier leadership stockpiled so that no freezer would ever go down waiting on a part.

One course of action is to put the company's oldest customer, a produce grower of fifteen years, on payment in advance and to sell the remaining receivables to a factoring firm at a discount. Cash would arrive within a week. The grower has already said it would move its business to a competitor, and the discount is money the company never gets back.

The other course of action is to leave customer terms alone and sell down the spare parts inventory, holding only the parts technicians replace most often and ordering the rest as they are needed. That cash comes back slowly, over months rather than a week, and it leaves the company exposed: one compressor failure with no spare on the shelf would spoil a customer's frozen stock, and the company would owe for the loss.

You have also found that a supplier invoice was entered twice in the closing books and overstated accounts payable. The chief executive officer (judge) wants your recommendation on which course of action to take, what the corrected entry does to the cash picture, and how the company would know afterward whether the decision was the right one. The chief executive officer (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer (judge) of NORTHRIDGE COLD CHAIN. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You took the company over fourteen months ago after two straight years of losses, and freeing cash is the difference between another lean year and a stable one. You want to hear which course of action the financial analyst recommends — payment in advance for the produce grower with the remaining receivables sold to a factoring firm, or selling down the spare parts inventory — and what the corrected supplier invoice does to the cash picture.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, what would tell you this was the right decision?
What would you watch in the first month to catch it going wrong?
